name: Donoghue v Stevenson
hinge: Whether a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer absent contractual privity
holding: A manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer — established the 'neighbour principle'
outcomeDeterminativeFact: The bottle was opaque, so no one had a chance to inspect it before consumption
keyFacts: A decomposed snail was found in a bottle of ginger beer
The bottle was opaque, preventing visual inspection
The plaintiff was not the purchaser — a friend bought the drink for her
No contract existed between the manufacturer and the plaintiff
ruleEstablished: Neighbour principle: you must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour

name: Winterbottom v Wright
hinge: Whether a party outside a contract can sue in negligence over a defective product
holding: No duty of care exists absent contractual privity — a third party injured by a defective product cannot recover in tort
outcomeDeterminativeFact: The plaintiff was a mail coach driver, not a party to the contract between the Postmaster-General and the coach supplier
keyFacts: The plaintiff was employed by the Postmaster-General to drive mail coaches
The defendant contracted with the Postmaster-General to supply and maintain coaches
A coach collapsed due to a latent defect, injuring the driver
No contract existed between the driver and the supplier
ruleEstablished: Privity of contract required for a duty of care (later displaced in product liability by Donoghue)

name: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co
hinge: Whether a public advertisement can constitute a binding unilateral offer
holding: Yes — a public advertisement can be a binding unilateral offer where the advertiser's language shows serious intent, and performance of the requested act constitutes acceptance
outcomeDeterminativeFact: The company's own advertisement stated that £1,000 was deposited with a specific bank to show sincerity of the offer
keyFacts: The Carbolic Smoke Ball Co advertised a reward of £100 to anyone who used their product and still caught influenza
The advertisement stated £1,000 was deposited with the Alliance Bank to show sincerity
Mrs Carlill used the smoke ball as directed and caught influenza
The company argued the advertisement was mere 'puff' and not a serious offer
ruleEstablished: A unilateral offer can be accepted by performance without prior notification where the terms clearly demonstrate an intention to be bound

name: Marbury v Madison
hinge: Whether the Supreme Court has the power to declare an act of Congress unconstitutional
holding: Yes — the Supreme Court has the power of judicial review to strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution
outcomeDeterminativeFact: Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 purported to expand the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction beyond what Article III of the Constitution permits
keyFacts: William Marbury was appointed as a justice of the peace in the final days of the Adams administration
His commission was not delivered before the new administration took office
Marbury petitioned the Supreme Court directly for a writ of mandamus to compel delivery
The Court found that Marbury was entitled to the commission, but the Court lacked jurisdiction
ruleEstablished: It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is — established judicial review

name: Brown v Board of Education
hinge: Whether segregated public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment
holding: Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal and violate the Equal Protection Clause — overruled Plessy v Ferguson's 'separate but equal' doctrine as applied to education
outcomeDeterminativeFact: The psychological evidence (doll studies) showed segregation instilled a sense of inferiority in Black children that affected their educational opportunity
keyFacts: Black children were denied admission to white public schools under state laws permitting racial segregation
The cases were consolidated from Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, and the District of Columbia
Expert psychological testimony demonstrated the harmful effects of segregation on children
The 'separate but equal' doctrine from Plessy v Ferguson (1896) had been the controlling precedent
ruleEstablished: In the field of public education, the doctrine of 'separate but equal' has no place — separate educational facilities are inherently unequal

name: Rylands v Fletcher
hinge: Whether a landowner is strictly liable when something they bring onto their land escapes and causes harm
holding: Yes — a person who brings onto their land something likely to do mischief if it escapes is strictly liable for all damage that is the natural consequence of its escape, regardless of negligence
outcomeDeterminativeFact: The defendants employed independent contractors to build a reservoir, and the contractors failed to seal disused mine shafts — water escaped into the plaintiff's mine
keyFacts: Rylands built a reservoir on his land to supply water to his mill
Unknown to him, the site contained disused mine shafts connected to Fletcher's adjoining mine
The contractors failed to properly seal the shafts
Water from the reservoir flooded Fletcher's mine
ruleEstablished: Strict liability for non-natural use of land — a person who brings or keeps a dangerous thing on their land is liable for damage caused by its escape

name: Palsgraf v Long Island Railroad Co.
hinge: Whether a defendant owes a duty of care to a plaintiff who was not within the foreseeable zone of danger
holding: No duty is owed to an unforeseeable plaintiff — the orbit of the danger as perceived by a reasonable person defines the scope of duty (Cardozo, majority)
outcomeDeterminativeFact: The railroad guards could not reasonably foresee that a dropped package of fireworks would explode and cause a scale to tip over on a passenger standing at the far end of the platform
keyFacts: Two guards helped a passenger board a moving train
The passenger dropped a package wrapped in newspaper
The package contained fireworks, which exploded on impact
The explosion caused scales at the far end of the platform to fall onto Mrs. Palsgraf
No one (including the guards) knew the package contained fireworks
ruleEstablished: Negligence requires a duty to the specific plaintiff — 'the risk reasonably to be perceived defines the duty to be obeyed' (Cardozo). Andrews' dissent argued that proximate cause, not duty, was the correct framework.
notableDissent: Judge Andrews — argued the focus should be on proximate causation ('was the harm a natural and probable consequence?'), not on duty to the specific plaintiff

name: Miranda v Arizona
hinge: Whether statements obtained during custodial interrogation are admissible without the suspect having been informed of the right to remain silent and the right to counsel
holding: No — the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination requires that a person taken into custody be warned that they have the right to remain silent, that anything they say can be used against them, that they have the right to an attorney, and that an attorney will be appointed if they cannot afford one
outcomeDeterminativeFact: Miranda was interrogated for two hours in police custody without being informed of his constitutional rights
keyFacts: Ernesto Miranda was arrested and taken into police custody for questioning
After two hours of interrogation, he signed a written confession
At no point was Miranda told he had the right to remain silent or to have an attorney
His confession was used at trial and he was convicted
The prosecution conceded Miranda was not advised of his rights
ruleEstablished: Procedural safeguards are necessary to secure the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination — police must give the now-famous 'Miranda warning' before custodial interrogation

name: Gideon v Wainwright
hinge: Whether the Sixth Amendment right to counsel in criminal cases applies to state courts through the Fourteenth Amendment
holding: Yes — the right to counsel is fundamental and essential to a fair trial; states must provide attorneys for indigent defendants in felony cases
outcomeDeterminativeFact: Clarence Earl Gideon, too poor to hire a lawyer, was forced to represent himself at trial, cross-examine witnesses, and make legal arguments without any legal training
keyFacts: Gideon was charged with breaking and entering a pool hall
He asked the trial judge to appoint a lawyer because he could not afford one
The judge refused — Florida law only allowed appointed counsel in capital cases
Gideon defended himself and was convicted
From prison, he hand-wrote a petition to the Supreme Court
ruleEstablished: The right of an indigent defendant to appointed counsel is a fundamental right essential to a fair trial, incorporated against the states via the Fourteenth Amendment. Overruled Betts v Brady (1942).

name: New York Times Co. v Sullivan
hinge: Whether a public official can recover damages for a defamatory falsehood relating to official conduct without proving the statement was made with 'actual malice'
holding: No — the First and Fourteenth Amendments require a public official suing for defamation to prove actual malice: that the statement was made with knowledge of its falsity or with reckless disregard for whether it was true or false
outcomeDeterminativeFact: The advertisement contained minor factual errors (e.g., students sang 'My Country 'Tis of Thee' not the National Anthem) that were not material to the core criticism of police conduct
keyFacts: Civil rights activists published a full-page ad in the NYT describing police actions against protesters in Montgomery, Alabama
The ad contained several minor factual inaccuracies
L.B. Sullivan, the Montgomery police commissioner, sued for libel even though he was not named in the ad
An Alabama jury awarded Sullivan $500,000
The actual number of times police 'ringed' the campus was wrong; the song students sang was wrong
ruleEstablished: The First Amendment protects criticism of public officials — a public official cannot recover damages for defamation absent proof of 'actual malice' (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth)

name: Plessy v Ferguson
hinge: Whether a state law mandating separate railway cars for Black and white passengers violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment
holding: No — 'separate but equal' accommodations do not violate the Equal Protection Clause. The Fourteenth Amendment was not intended to abolish distinctions based on color or to enforce social equality
outcomeDeterminativeFact: The Court reasoned that enforced separation does not stamp either race with a badge of inferiority — if members of the affected race feel inferior, 'it is not by reason of anything found in the act, but solely because the colored race chooses to put that construction upon it'
keyFacts: Homer Plessy, who was seven-eighths white, boarded a white-only railway car in Louisiana
He was arrested under Louisiana's Separate Car Act (1890)
Plessy argued the law violated the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments
The Court upheld the Louisiana law 7-1 (Justice Harlan dissented)
ruleEstablished: The 'separate but equal' doctrine — racial segregation is constitutional as long as the separate facilities are equal. Overruled by Brown v Board of Education (1954).
notableDissent: Justice John Marshall Harlan — 'Our constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.' The majority's holding will prove as 'pernicious' as Dred Scott.

name: Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.
hinge: Whether courts must defer to a federal agency's reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute the agency administers
holding: Yes — established 'Chevron deference': Step 1 — if the statute is clear, that is the end of the matter; Step 2 — if the statute is ambiguous, the court must defer to the agency's reasonable interpretation
outcomeDeterminativeFact: Congress had not directly addressed whether a 'stationary source' under the Clean Air Act meant each individual smokestack or an entire industrial plant — the EPA interpreted it as the latter, and the Court held that was a permissible construction of the ambiguous term
keyFacts: The Clean Air Act required states to regulate 'stationary sources' of pollution
The EPA interpreted this to mean an entire industrial plant could be treated as one source (the 'bubble concept')
The NRDC argued each individual emission point within a plant was a separate source
The Court found Congress had not clearly defined the term
ruleEstablished: Courts apply a two-step framework when reviewing agency interpretations: (1) if Congress has spoken clearly, that controls; (2) if the statute is ambiguous, courts defer to the agency's reasonable interpretation — called 'Chevron deference'
